articles.title: Iran to declare Hormuz restricted zone, warns of 'more painful' attack response
articles.description: The planned restricted zone adds a fresh layer of shipping risk to the Strait of Hormuz corridor, through which a fifth of global oil supply moved before the conflict. Any expansion of sanctionable shipping areas raises the prospect of further disruption to tanker traffic and insurance costs, even as US officials maintain that transit volumes remain close to two thirds of pre-war levels. The explicit threat of a "faster, heavier and more painful" response to further attacks keeps a geopolitical risk premium embedded in oil prices, particularly given the string of tit-for-tat strikes since the weekend. Traders will watch for the zone's actual coordinates and enforcement mechanism once published, since the scale of any premium depends on how much additional shipping area is affected. --- Despite the US holiday Monday Globex will open for oil trade at 6pm US Eastern time Sunday, which is 2200 GMT. Early FX rates often give an early indication to changes in sentiment regarding weekend news flow. So far its realtively calm despite this jawboning from Iran: Monday open indicative forex prices, 07 September 2026 Iran warns of tougher response: Oil, gold and stocks to watch over the holiday weekend --- Iran is preparing to widen its sanctionable shipping zone near Hormuz just as its officials warn Washington that further strikes will trigger a far heavier retaliation. Summary: Iran's top security official says a restricted zone will be announced outside the Strait of Hormuz in coming days, starting from the line of the US Navy's blockade Any ship entering the new zone will reportedly be added to a sanctions list Maps of ship passage through Hormuz, agreed with Oman, are due to be signed in coming days Parliament Speaker Qalibaf says any future attack on Iran's interests will draw a faster, heavier and more painful response The warning follows US strikes on three Iranian vessels after Iran's Revolutionary Guard fired ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships A June ceasefire has unravelled, with tit-for-tat strikes resuming after a pause through most of August Iran is preparing to announce a new restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz within days, according to Reuters, as its top security official warned that any ship entering the area will be added to a sanctions list. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said the zone would begin from the line of the US Navy's blockade and extend into parts of the Gulf, according to state media, with maps of shipping passage agreed with Oman due to be signed in the coming days. The move lands alongside a sharper rhetorical warning from Tehran. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said the rules of the game had changed, telling the US that any future attack on Iran's interests and security "will receive a faster, heavier and more painful response." The comments follow a fresh round of hostilities: US Central Command said it struck three Iranian vessels, including one off Kharg Island, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps fired ballistic missiles at two US Navy ships. Six months into the conflict, the situation remains at a stalemate. A preliminary ceasefire reached in June has unravelled, and diplomatic efforts to revive it have made little progress. Strikes paused for much of August before resuming in recent days. Iran retains the capacity to threaten US interests in the region and to further restrict flows through Hormuz, a corridor that carried a fifth of global oil supply before the war. US officials maintain that enforcement of Washington's own blockade is holding: Energy Secretary Chris Wright said transits through the strait are averaging more than 9 million barrels a day, putting flows at roughly two thirds of pre-conflict levels once alternative pipeline routes are included. Whether Iran's new zone meaningfully adds to that pressure will depend on its precise boundaries and how strictly it is enforced once published, details that were not yet available at the time of the announcement. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
